PROLOGUE

If one considers carefully the evangelical and apostolic preaching, one will find
quite clearly that the preaching of the Catholic preachers must deal with vices
and virtues: persuading toward one and dissuading from the other. And most continually it must be
to persuade them toward the theological virtues, and dissuade them from the vices contrary
to these (and on this there is much material in the first six books of this history; and
in the postil on the epistles and gospels for the Sundays of the whole year, which I
made; and much more fully in the Christian Doctrine, which the first twelve
preachers preached to this Indian people, which I, as an eyewitness,
compiled in this Mexican language). And in order to give greater opportunity and help
to the preachers of this new Church, in this volume I have dealt with the
moral virtues according to the understanding, practice, and language that these same people
have of them. I have not followed in this treatise the order that other writers have used
in treating this subject matter, but instead follow the order of the persons, dignities, and offices
and occupations that exist among this people, setting forth the goodness of each person and then
their wickedness, with an abundance of nouns, adjectives, and verbs (where there is great
abundance of language very proper and very common among them). There are also
contained, in this same style, in this volume, all the parts of the body, both
internal and external, in great detail; and after this, most of the illnesses
to which human bodies are subject in this land, and the remedies
against them; and along with this, nearly all the generations that have come
to settle this land.

Here begins the tenth book of the General History, in which are treated the vices and virtues, both spiritual and corporal, of every kind of person.

Chapter One, on the qualities and conditions of persons related by kinship.

The father is the first root and stock of kinship. The proper quality of a good father is to be diligent and careful, that with perseverance he maintain his household and sustain it.
The good father rears and maintains his children, gives them a good upbringing and instruction, corrects them, gives them good examples and good counsel, and stores up treasure for them, and keeps watch over them; he keeps account of the expenses of his household, and regulates his children's spending, and provides for things to come.

The quality of a bad father is to be lazy, careless, idle; he looks after no one, he lacks the diligence to do what he is obliged to do, and he wastes his time in vain.

[fo. 1]

Here is the tenth book, which treats of the General History: here are told the various virtues, both good and evil, and all the vices and good customs that are practiced, and by these our hearts are known — whoever does them.

Here is the first chapter, in which is told the manner and condition of life of those who are joined together by ties of blood kinship.

The father, the parent, is the true root of kinship, the origin of lineage; he is the heart of the father's line; he is one who receives, who loves, who is attentive, who is anxious, who is burdened, who worries, who is responsible, who cares for others.

He rears, he nurtures, he raises up, he teaches, he admonishes, he instructs, he guides the life of his children; he sets up a bright mirror for them, he holds before them a great burning torch; he is attentive, he corrects, he disciplines, he watches over, he is mindful, he is prudent, he looks far ahead, he is thoughtful, he settles matters, he puts things in order.

As for the bad father, the negligent one, the lazy one: he does not care for anyone, he is thoughtless, he is careless, he does no good for his children, he abandons them, he neglects them, he lets things go undone, he leaves them forsaken.

Book Ten

The quality proper to the mother is
to have children, and give them milk; the
virtuous mother is watchful and quick, she does not
stop, she is diligent, a watcher, solicitous and
anxious. She raises her children, is continually
caring for them, has vigilance, lacks nothing,
she pampers them, she is like a light for
everyone in her house, she becomes anxious
over the needs of each one, and no
necessary thing in the house is neglected;
she is a keeper of order, she is industrious, or
hard-working.

The bad mother is foolish, ignorant,
sleepy, lazy, wasteful,
a person of poor management, careless
of her house, she lets things be lost
through laziness or anger; she does not attend to
the needs of those in her house, she does not
look after the things of her house, she does not
correct the faults of those in her house: and for
that reason she grows worse every day —.

She raises her children strictly, cares for them

The bad mother is wicked,

The child, the offspring, the child

The good child is one who respects people,

who is grateful, who honors
others, who shows reverence, who treats people well

Of vices and virtues.

Customs, and in body, a child resembles his father or his mother.

The vicious son.

The bad son is mischievous, rebellious, or disobedient, crazy, mischievous, unreceptive to good counsel; he throws good doctrine behind his back; he is restless, dissolute, boastful, vainglorious, ill-bred, uncouth or rough; he receives no good teaching. The good counsels of his father and his mother go in one ear and out the other; even if he is whipped, and even if he is beaten, he does not for that reason mend his ways.

The virtuous daughter.

The young woman or daughter who is raised in her father's house has these good qualities: she is truly a virgin, never known by a man; she is obedient, modest, intelligent, able; a noble woman, honored, respected, well brought up, instructed, taught; a person who is advised, warned, and kept watch over.

And virtues. Folio 2.

[Continuing from the previous page] ...she is trustworthy, discreet, generous, good-hearted, gracious; she makes things known to others, she visits and speaks with people.

The vicious child, the wretched son, is utterly wretched, stubborn, hard-hearted, of evil heart, wretched of heart, hollow-headed, deaf to advice, wayward, wide-eyed with fright, foolish, proud, muddled, one who must constantly be talked to and corrected, foolish, ungrateful, taking nothing to heart, neither his mother's nor his father's words. He goes about causing trouble on every side; he thrusts his hand even into the ears of those who try to raise and discipline him; he is like a stinging nettle wherever he looks; no one respects him; he lives frivolously, he lives restlessly, he opens his eyes wide in mischief, he mocks things, he twists things about, he perverts things.

The modest young woman, the reared maiden, the well-brought-up maiden, who truly is a maiden in body and soul — she is good, virtuous; a good maiden is obedient, discreet, attentive, prudent, of good understanding, dignified, respectable, worthy of honor and fear, well counseled, well reared, well taught, well instructed, of pure and good life, modest.

Folio 4.

Book Ten

The vicious daughter.

The bad or wicked daughter is bad in her body: dissolute, loose, a whore, over-dressed, she goes about showing off, adorning herself with excessive care, wandering through the streets, giving herself over to the vices of the flesh; she goes about like a flower picked at the roadside — her whole life and pleasure consists of wandering like a weed by the wayside; she goes about like a madwoman.

Spoiled son or daughter.

A boy or girl who takes after his or her family's lineage, noble or generous — a delicate, pampered, tender, and beautiful daughter.
The eldest daughter is called the firstborn; the second daughter; the third daughter; the last daughter. The prudent reader should not take offense that only words, and not full sentences, are given here, as was done above; in other parts further on [sentences will be given], because the main purpose of this treatise is to apply the Castilian language to the Indian language, so that people may learn to speak the proper words concerning this subject of vices and virtues.

A virtuous boy or girl.

A boy or girl of good character is diligent, lively, sharp-witted, quick, moderate, discreet, and obedient, who willingly does what he is told.

A vicious boy.

The wicked boy has these traits: he is lazy, slow, fat and clumsy, foolish, stupid, coarse, and indiscreet, understanding things backwards.

Great-grandmother.

The great-grandmother is a figure of old age,
she is like a child in her condition: the good
great-grandmother is worthy of being praised,
worthy that one be grateful to her for the good
she did for her descendants; it is a glory
to her descendants to be named
after her, as great-grandmother, for she is the origin
of the lineage or family line. The bad great-
grandmother is detestable; no one willingly hears
her name, her presence
or her memory provokes nausea or disgust,
and causes anger.

Great-great-grandfather.
The great-great-grandfather and great-great-grandmother tremble
in the head, and the body is always
coughing, walks bent over, grows weak,
and is at the very end of old age. The good
great-great-grandfather, or great-great-grandmother, stands in
the place of father and mother to their descendants,
is like a precious root or foundation.
The bad great-great-grandfather, or great-great-grandmother, is
a worthless old person, a worthless root, cast aside, who lived a
bad life, leaving his or her own with nothing good to remember.

Of the vices
Grandson or granddaughter.
¶The grandson or granddaughter is loved, is
cherished, is esteemed; he proceeds
from his ancestors, like the thorns
on which one is born, or like the chips
left from the stone that is carved, or like
the kernels of the ear of corn, the adopted one
called "cacamatl," a crumb,
alive, precious, like a precious stone,
like fine plumage; imitators
of their own kin, in bearing and in
deeds. The good grandson follows the
good examples of his own people; he is
a living image of them, he brings
honor to his own, with his good
life he blossoms like a flower among
his own. The mischievous grandson
dishonors his own, scatters to dust
the honor of his own: he is dissolute
and self-willed, takes no one's
opinion on what he must
say; he governs himself however he
pleases, judges as he fancies,
he is conceited, villainous, and utterly arrogant.

Chapter two, on the
degrees of affinity.
Father-in-law.
¶The father-in-law is he who has
a son-in-law or daughter-in-law; if they are living (so called); if they are dead,
he is called "miccamontatli."
The father-in-law seeks out a wife for
his son, and marries off his daughters, and
takes care of his grandchildren.
The good father-in-law takes care to
give his son-in-law what he needs,
and to settle his daughter-in-law in
his house.
The bad father-in-law always holds hatred
toward his daughter-in-law or his son, between his
daughter and his son-in-law; he wants no one
to stay in his house — he is stingy, miserly.

rules.

DEGREE OF AFFINITY
¶Father-in-law, deceased father-in-law, mother-in-law,
son-in-law, one who takes a son-in-law, one who takes a daughter-in-law,
one who gives a daughter in marriage. He seeks, he looks for,
he arranges marriages, he arranges marriages. The good father-in-law
loves people, he establishes a household for them, he embraces them,
he takes them into his arms. The bad, unfortunate father-in-law is one who
sows discord between people, who divides them,
who scatters them about; no one wants him near, he is stingy, quarrelsome.

Book Ten

Mother-in-law.
The mother-in-law does, on her part, for her children, everything that was said about the father-in-law. The good mother-in-law watches over her daughter-in-law and guards her discreetly. The bad mother-in-law rejoices if her daughter-in-law is of poor account, is a waster of her own and others' property, and is unfaithful to her daughter-in-law.

Father of the father-in-law.
The honored father, or father of the father-in-law, has all the qualities that were said of the father-in-law. The good lord is rich and has gained much through his labor. The bad lord-father, or poor one, is stingy, useless, and never leaves his corner.

Mother of the father-in-law, or mother-in-law.
The honored mother, mother of the father-in-law or mother-in-law, has the same qualities as the mother-in-law. The good honored mother is an old, honored, lovable, and venerable woman. The bad honored mother harms herself and her family, leaving debts that her successors must later pay.

Son-in-law.
The son-in-law is a young married man, exempt from the order of the tlamacazque and telpuchtli. The good son-in-law is respectful, reverent, and loved by his parents-in-law. The bad son-in-law is shameless, grasping, or covetous; he steals what he can from his father-in-law's house and lives in concubinage.

Daughter-in-law.
The daughter-in-law is formally requested in marriage, a legitimate wife; the good daughter-in-law is not gossipy
